title: Our houses are exposed, they said. They only wanted to flee.
subtitle: An excuse that hid the real reason
then: During the siege, some told the people of Madinah to go home. Ibn Abbas said a group asked permission, saying {trap}we fear our homes may be robbed{/trap}. Allah said their homes were not exposed. {trap}They only wanted to run{/trap} from where they were needed.
now: The volunteer rota at the masjid, the family member who needs a carer this weekend. Suddenly you have a work thing. {idea}Allah knows the real reason{/idea} behind the excuse, even when you half-believe it yourself.
old: My excuse is valid, so I am off the hook.
new: Allah sees whether my reason is real or just a way to escape.
try: Next time you reach for an excuse, ask yourself honestly what the real reason is.

title: Faith that would fold at the first real pressure.
subtitle: How shallow commitment behaves
then: Ibn Kathir, citing Qatadah and Ibn Jarir, says if the enemy had entered and demanded disbelief, {trap}they would have given in promptly{/trap}. They would not stay firm {trap}if faced with the slightest fear{/trap}.
now: The new job where drinks after work are expected. The friends who laugh when you step out to pray. {idea}Pressure is quiet, not dramatic.{/idea} Faith with roots is built before the test arrives.
old: I will be strong when a real test comes.
new: Firmness is built in small daily choices, before the big test.
try: Practise one small act of faith in public today that you usually hide.

title: They had promised Allah. A promise to Him is asked about.
subtitle: Covenants made in calm times
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah reminds them of {idea}the promise they made before the fear struck{/idea}: that they would not turn their backs. {trap}Allah will inevitably ask them about that covenant.{/trap}
now: Ramadan, when you promised yourself you would keep praying Fajr. The hospital visit when you swore you would call your father more. {idea}Those were promises to Allah too.{/idea} He will ask about them.
old: Promises I made in emotional moments do not really count.
new: A promise to Allah is remembered and asked about, even if I forget it.
try: Pick one promise to Allah from a past Ramadan and restart it today, small.

title: Running from death does not buy you more time.
subtitle: Fleeing changes nothing about your appointed term
then: Ibn Kathir says fleeing {idea}will not delay their appointed end or lengthen their lives{/idea}. It may even bring it sooner. He links it to 4:77: {reward}the enjoyment of this world is short, the Hereafter is better{/reward}.
now: You avoid the hard conversation, the hospital visit, the responsibility, as if dodging them keeps you safe. {idea}Your time is already written.{/idea} What you do with it is the part you choose.
old: If I avoid every hard thing, I will be safer.
new: My time is set by Allah, so running from duty buys me nothing.
try: Do one thing today you have been avoiding out of fear.

title: Who can shield you from Allah, if He wills harm or mercy?
subtitle: No protector or helper but Him
then: Ibn Kathir says {idea}they have no one except Allah to respond to their cries{/idea}. Those fleeing the trench imagined safety elsewhere. But no one can block what He wills, {reward}whether harm or mercy{/reward}.
now: The mercy you are waiting for: a job, a child, healing. No one can stop it if He wills it. {reward}And no one can give it if He does not.{/reward} So the only place to run is to Him.
old: If I find the right person, they can protect me from anything.
new: Only Allah can block harm or send mercy, so I run to Him.
try: Ask Allah directly today for one mercy you have been waiting for.

title: Allah knows who holds others back from doing good.
subtitle: The ones who say come here, stay comfortable
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah's knowledge covers those who {trap}told others not to go out{/trap}, saying to friends: come to us, to {trap}the shade and the fruits{/trap}. They themselves came to the battle only a little.
now: Your friend is about to start memorising Qur'an, or volunteer on weekends. You say: relax, you do too much. {idea}Notice when you are the voice holding someone back.{/idea}
old: Talking someone out of a hard good deed is just being caring.
new: Allah knows when I hold others back from good, even gently.
try: Encourage one person today in a good thing they are trying to do.

title: Frozen in fear, then sharp-tongued once it is safe.
subtitle: Cowardice in danger, boasting after
then: Ibn Kathir says when security returned, they spoke eloquently, {trap}claiming they were the bravest{/trap}. Qatadah said at sharing time they were the loudest: {trap}give us, we were there with you{/trap}. In battle they had been the most absent.
now: The group project where one person vanished, then presented the slides. The family crisis where someone showed up only for the will reading. {idea}Check whether you are ever that person.{/idea}
old: I can take credit as long as I was around.
new: Quiet presence in hard times matters more than loud claims later.
try: Give credit today to someone who did work that you might be praised for.

title: They wished to be far away, asking for news from a distance.
subtitle: Watching from the sidelines
then: Ibn Kathir says even after the Confederates left, they thought {trap}the armies were still nearby{/trap}. If they came back, these men would rather be {trap}out in the desert asking for news{/trap} than with the believers in Madinah.
now: A relative is sick and you follow it on the family group chat, never visiting. A friend is struggling and you just watch their stories. {idea}Asking for news from far away is not the same as being there.{/idea}
old: Keeping updated from a distance is enough support.
new: Being present when it is hard is what loyalty means.
try: Visit or call someone going through a hard time, instead of just checking updates.

title: In the Messenger of Allah ﷺ you have the best example.
subtitle: For whoever hopes in Allah and remembers Him much
then: Ibn Kathir calls this {idea}an important principle: follow the Messenger ﷺ in his words and deeds{/idea}. At Al-Ahzab, people were told to copy his {reward}patience, guarding, striving and waiting for Allah's way out{/reward}. It was said to those who panicked.
now: Crisis at work, panic in the family chat, everyone shouting. You ask: what would he ﷺ do here? {idea}Patient, present, working, trusting.{/idea} That question changes how you walk into the room.
old: The Prophet's ﷺ example is for worship, not for crises at work.
new: His example covers how I act under pressure, every day.
try: In your next stressful moment, pause and ask how the Prophet ﷺ would respond.

title: Seeing the armies, the believers said: this is what was promised.
subtitle: Hardship that increased faith
then: Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said the believers remembered 2:214: {idea}trials come, then the help of Allah is near{/idea}. So seeing the armies {reward}only added to their faith{/reward}. Ibn Kathir notes that faith can increase and decrease.
now: The same layoff email reaches two colleagues. One says Allah has abandoned me. The other says I was told life would test me, and help is near. {reward}Same email, different heart.{/reward}
old: Hardship means my faith is failing.
new: Hardship can be the very thing that grows my faith, if I read it right.
try: When something hard happens today, say: this is what Allah and His Messenger promised.
